newsitem.title: UK: No short cut to investment bank success- M.Stanley.
newsitem.headline: No short cut to investment bank success- M.Stanley.

text.p: European banks pushing to make their mark in the world of investment banking are misguided in their attempts to lure big hitters with telephone number salaries, a senior U.S. investment banker said on Wednesday.

"It is very hard to do this in any reasonable period of time by simply adding people at above market compensation levels," Richard Fisher, chairman of Morgan Stanley Dean Witter Discover told an industry conference.
Morgan Stanley's $10.6 billion merger with Dean Witter Discover & Co in February, has created the largest U.S. securities firm in terms of market worth.
Fisher admitted Morgan Stanley had looked at 13 possible merger candidates before deciding on its future spouse, a list he said had included some surprising choices.

But without naming any firms, he cast doubt over the strategy employed those such as Britain's Barclays Plc whose BZW investment banking arm has attempted its assault on the world's markets with a hiring drive.

"This group attempting to put in place a global investment banking capability are finding out it is not something you accomplish easily or quickly," Fisher told the three-day Global Borrowers and Investors Forum.

While the influx of large, well-financed European competitors would have an impact on margins, Fisher described their influence would be medium term as they were market share oriented rather than financial return oriented.

The debate over how European firms can seize the initiative from the "Bulge Bracket" Wall Street securities firms resurfaced this week with the sudden departure of NatWest Markets boss Martin Owen and a major strategic review at the investment banking wing of Britain's NatWest Bank.

Fisher outlined his vision of the brave new world of investment banking, which he said would be driven by the increasing complexity of financial markets and products as well as technology, innovation, globalisation and deregulation.
"The work we do and the work our clients and customers do is becoming more difficult and that really is the best possible thing for our business."
"As long as the world is getting more complex --and we think it will -- that will create opportunities for firms that are well-positioned."
And investment banking would become increasingly capital intensive in the years ahead and combined with the importance of technology, backing Fisher's argument for size and scale.
"We believe technology is going to be a competitive issue," he said, adding it was no longer a support function but an integral frontline area.

Underlining this was Morgan Stanley's own 1997 budget proposal for technology which totalled $830 million, but had been trimmed to "somewhat less", Fisher said, adding he had been stunned by the cost required to keep his firm in the game.
"The business is going to be extraordinarily competitive. Its going to take size, scale and success in technology," he added.
And already intense competition would become even more fierce as new challengers arose from a more interesting group of competitors.
"Our business and the insurance business is converging, we are more and more called on to price longer term risk and more and more in the asset management business."
"We expect the very large global insurance companies to be very much more significant competitors in the next five years," he said.

Fisher also believes Glass-Steagall act which prevents commercial banks owning securities firms will disappear, paving the way for "some staggeringly surprising combinations" as a wave of consolidation continues.

This was likely to involve large securities firms buying small banks and further huge mergers such as the coming together of Chemical Bank and Chase Manhattan Corp, aimed at reducing capacity and employing less capital.
Fisher is optimistic about his merged firm's future. He said it would increase its exposure to financial businesses, achieve scale and create value for stockholders while remaining independent.
Cost reductions had not been the driving force for the decision to combine with Dean Witter Discover, but the merged group would aggressively pursue any savings it could.
Far more important, he said, was the group could make a significant impact on the return on equity by improving the capital efficiency of the combined business, without altering its credit ratings.

"We believe that we can take between $2.0 and $2.5 billion of capital out the combined business...the impact on the return on equity is very substantial. We think there are extraordinary capital efficiency opportunities," he said.
